subcategory: Western US native dry spring bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs or bulb scales in fall into coarse, well-drained sandy or loamy soil; withhold water completely once foliage yellows in early summer.

directions: A dainty, subtly beautiful western-US native for rock gardens and bulb frames, this fritillary's mottled purple-brown-and-yellow bells add quiet texture among larger spring bulbs without competing for attention. Plant in coarse, well-drained soil that mimics its native montane slopes and open forest understories, giving it a normal winter-wet, spring-growth cycle before withholding water completely once foliage yellows. A raised bed or bulb frame with sharp drainage suits it better than a typical perennial border.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in dappled shade under oaks or conifers in heavy, sometimes serpentine-derived soil that stays moist through winter and spring, then dries for summer. Source only nursery-propagated bulbs, never wild-collected material.

directions: A northern-California woodland geophyte with mahogany-and-yellow mottled flowers, this fritillary is useful for shaded native plantings and as a conservation-minded alternative to the more commonly grown species in the genus. It is CNPS rare-plant-listed in parts of its range, so source only nursery-propagated bulbs. Because it occupies a hybrid-swarm zone with other California fritillaries, keep seed lots isolated if growing alongside related species to preserve identity.

planting.note: Plant bulbs from a reputable propagating nursery into heavier, slow-draining adobe clay soil; avoid summer irrigation and protect from gophers.

directions: One of the few fragrant fritillaries, this species carries pale pink, dark-striped bells with real scent, a striking choice for gardeners wanting to grow a California-endemic rarity responsibly from nursery stock. It naturally grows in sticky adobe clay in the southern Sierra foothills and Tehachapi area, so a heavier, slow-draining soil actually suits it better than the sharp drainage most fritillaries want. It is state-listed as Threatened, so only plant bulbs from a reputable propagating nursery and keep competing turf or weeds away.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in well-drained gritty soil at the edge of a light-canopy planting; stake lightly in open sites or let it lean into companion shrubs given its unusual height for the genus.

directions: Unusually tall for the genus, reaching four to five feet, this fritillary carries whorled narrow leaves and multiple small nodding purple-to-green bells per stem, a striking architectural native for a Sierra-foothill-style dry woodland garden. Give it well-drained gritty soil at the edge of a light-canopy planting, replicating the Red Fir and Yellow Pine forest margins it grows in naturally in the Sierra Nevada. Let foliage die back untouched and keep the site dry from early summer through fall dormancy.

planting.note: Divide bulbs during fall dormancy and plant in ordinary, even meager, well-drained garden soil; top-dress with grit periodically rather than replanting deep, since bulbs work toward the surface over time.

directions: An easy, vigorous East Asian species bearing up to six greenish-white bells per stem on whorled foliage, this fritillary is more tolerant of garden conditions than many alpine-house species, making it a good gateway fritillary for growers new to the genus. It tolerates less-than-perfect drainage better than most fritillaries and has naturalized well in cold-frame and rock-garden settings. Avoid soggy winter sites, which remain its one real limiting factor.

planting.note: Grow in a bulb frame or alpine house in rich, peaty, sharply drained compost; water sparingly from mid-autumn, increasing once shoots emerge, then tapering off through late spring dormancy.

directions: A compact Caucasus, Turkey, and Iran alpine with broad glossy gray-green leaves and a single dark maroon-purple, strongly checkered bell, this fritillary gives good scale and color contrast for a scree bed or trough. In climates without a naturally dry, Mediterranean-type summer, give it overhead rain protection or plant among shrub or tree roots that pull soil moisture down in summer. It produces bulbils freely, making vegetative increase faster than for most fritillaries.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a cool spot that doesn't bake in summer; give a cold winter rest in pots but avoid bone-dry summer treatment.

directions: An understated but elegant alpine species with a blue-grey bloom outside and dark reddish-purple within a single rounded bell, this fritillary makes a good subtle companion among showier spring bulbs in a cool rock garden. It comes from subalpine meadows and shady limestone ledges rather than scorching scree, and tolerates hard frost well, native to elevations above Erzurum, Turkey. It can emerge quite early in winter in mild climates without damage.

planting.note: Divide offsets in late summer dormancy, or plant in a scree bed, raised bed, or terracotta pan in full sun with fertile but sharply drained soil.

directions: Compact and clump-forming, this fritillary carries clusters of bright yellow-and-lime nodding bells over fleshy gray-green leaves, one of the more cheerful-colored small fritillaries, well suited to sunny rock gardens or pans. Native to mountain scree in southwest Turkey and the Greek islands, it wants fertile but sharply drained soil in full sun. Watch for slugs and lily beetle, which are its main pest issues in cultivation; otherwise it's largely trouble-free.

planting.note: Plant the large bulb on its side at about four times its own diameter in depth in a bulb frame or raised bed with a rain cover during summer dormancy, to prevent rot.

directions: A distinctive Central Asian species with up to ten nodding, widely flared, greenish-yellow-to-purple-brown bells on thick glaucous foliage, this fritillary gives real textural contrast in a spring bulb collection, unlike the typical narrow fritillary bell shape. Coming from areas with cold winters under snow and hot, dry summers, it performs best in a bulb frame or raised bed with a rain cover during summer dormancy. The bulb itself is reportedly rodent-resistant, a nice bonus where squirrels or voles raid other spring bulbs.
